contributions.headingText: Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma (FDCS) is a malignant neoplasm showing morphological and phenotypic characteristics of follicular dendritic cells (FDCs), which are stroma-derived cells normally found in germinal centres.

FDCS occurs in extranodal sites (in 58% of cases), lymph nodes (in 31%), or as concomitant nodal and extranodal disease (in 10%) {23755890}. Extranodal disease occurs most commonly in the abdomen (particularly in the gastrointestinal tract and retroperitoneum) and upper aerodigestive tract, but it may occur at almost any extranodal site {32905993; 20503450; 32991350}. Nodal disease is most common in cervical and abdominal lymph nodes {23755890}.

Most patients present with a slow-growing, painless mass and/or isolated lymphadenopathy {23755890; 26910224; 31205436}. Patients with abdominal disease may present with abdominal pain, and rare systemic symptoms can include fatigue, fever, and night sweats. FDCS can be associated with hyaline-vascular Castleman disease (HVCD) (see section Unicentric Castleman disease) or with autoimmune diseases (including paraneoplastic pemphigus / paraneoplastic autoimmune multiorgan syndrome and myasthenia gravis) {30222603; 16120143; 10025851; 16029358}.

FDCS is rare {9010103; 12121233; 9737236; 2420185; 8712294; 2158241} and can occur at any age (median: 50 years). There is no sex predilection. FDCS may be more frequent among certain ethnic groups or geographical locations, with the tumour being disproportionally frequently reported from eastern Asia {26910224; 23755890}.

A subset (< 20%) of cases are associated with HVCD {8172326; 9351567; 11422494; 27318412}, which can precede or co-occur with FDCS. The presence of dysplastic FDCs outside the follicles in HVCD is suggestive of transformation from this population, which may explain the association between HVCD and FDCS {27206572; 28695297}.

Non-neoplastic FDCs are derived from perivascular progenitors (vascular mural cells) rather than haematopoietic precursors {22770220}. A hyperplasia–dysplasia–neoplasia model of FDC proliferation has been proposed for the link between HVCD and FDCS, as supported by the shared clonality and EGFR (HER1) overexpression in dysplastic FDCs and FDCS {14562277; 23888072}.

Cytogenetic studies have shown a complex karyotype {23422480}. Genomic studies show recurrent alterations in NF-κB pathway genes (BIRC3, NFKBIA, TRAF3, SOCS3, CYLD, and TNFAIP3) in 40–60% of cases, and in tumour suppressor genes (CDKN2A, RB1, and TP53) in 20–30% of cases {26564005; 28621320; 33904632}. A small subset of cases was reported to harbour IG rearrangement {19145200} or BRAF p.V600E mutation {24720374}. Other uncommon genetic alterations include HDGFRP3 (HDGFL3)::SHC4 fusion {28975018}, focal deletion of JAK2 and BRAF {29496669}, and focal copy-number gain of CD274 (PDL1) and PDCD1LG2 (PDL2) {26564005}. Transcriptomic analysis has shown highly specific expression of FDCSP and SRGN; a microenvironment enriched in T follicular helper (TFH) and T regulatory (Treg) cells; and upregulation of PD1, PDL1, and PDL2 {28130401; 28145886}.

FDCS is usually well-circumscribed and sometimes encapsulated, with a bosselated or nodular appearance. Tumour size ranges from 10 to 150 mm depending upon the anatomical location, with the largest tumours reported in the abdomen and mediastinum {26910224; 8712294; 32905993}. The cut surface is solid and tan to grey-white. Haemorrhage and necrosis can be seen in large tumours.

The neoplastic cells show a spindled, ovoid, or epithelioid cell morphology and are arranged in whorls, fascicles, syncytial sheets, and nodules, and in a storiform pattern. Several patterns can be seen in the same tumour. Tumour cells have moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm with indistinct cell borders, creating a syncytial appearance. The nuclei are elongated, with vesicular chromatin, delicate nuclear membranes, and small but distinct nucleoli. The nuclei tend to be unevenly spaced and clustered. Intranuclear pseudoinclusions are common. Binucleated forms reminiscent of benign FDCs may be present and represent a helpful diagnostic clue. Some cases may show prominent cytological atypia, with multinucleation and pleomorphic nuclei.

Typically, there is a light infiltrate of small lymphocytes among the tumour cells {32991350}. Lymphoid aggregates can be seen at the periphery of the tumour or around blood vessels. Neutrophils or eosinophils may be seen, along with dilated and thick hyalinized blood vessels {26910224; 32991350; 11796841}.

Less common morphological features include epithelioid tumour cells with hyaline cytoplasm; clear cells; myxoid stroma; fluid-filled cystic spaces; prominent fibrovascular septa; and admixed multinucleated, Reed–Sternberg–like or osteoclast-like giant cells {15252304; 9010103; 8712294; 9606805}. Cases showing jigsaw puzzle–like lobulation and perivascular spaces, mimicking thymoma or thymic carcinoma, have been reported {10931467}.

Immunohistochemistry

FDCS expresses antigens characteristic of normal FDCs, including CD21, CD23, CD35, clusterin, CXCL13, podoplanin (recognized by D2-40), and SSTR2 {12121233; 15252304; 17373675; 17951199; 18792075; 25310210; 26564005; 28695297; 30585825}, and the newer markers FDCSP and SRGN {28145886}. Among these markers, CXCL13, CD21, and clusterin are expressed most often (80–90% of cases) {15467709; 28145886}. CXCL13 and the complement and Fc receptors (CD21, CD35, and CD23) show the highest specificity for FDCS {28145886}. FDCS is also generally positive for fascin, PDL1, desmoplakin, EGFR, and vimentin {15252304; 28695297}. There are occasional reports of positivity for CD4, CD30, CD31, CD45, CD68, CD163, claudin-4, EMA, lysozyme, S100, and vimentin {32547956; 28695297}. Expression of CD20, cytokeratin, or thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF1) is exceptional {21836499; 12121233; 31205436}. The Ki-67 proliferation index is highly variable (5–70%) {28695297}.

The admixed small lymphocytes can be predominantly T cells, predominantly B cells, or a mixture of T and B cells {9010103}. In almost half of all cases, an indolent T-lymphoblastic proliferation (see section Indolent T-lymphoblastic proliferation) is present {23060347; 19740517}, with an infiltrate rich in TdT-positive cells that correlates with the occurrence of paraneoplastic manifestations {30222603}.

Differential diagnosis

FDCS can mimic a wide variety of tumour types, such as unclassified pleomorphic sarcoma, meningioma, thymoma, thymic carcinoma, angiosarcoma, undifferentiated carcinoma, lymphoepithelial carcinoma, and gastrointestinal stromal tumour. The diagnostic problem can often be solved by applying a panel of immunohistochemical markers.

Cytomorphological analysis coupled with ancillary techniques on fine-needle aspirate cell blocks is highly effective for diagnosis {15584048; 29275417; 33493367}. Spindle to ovoid cells are arranged in clusters in a background of small lymphocytes. Single scattered tumour cells can also be seen. The cells show a moderate amount of cytoplasm and finely granular to vesicular nuclear chromatin with prominent nucleoli. Occasional intranuclear pseudoinclusions and nuclear grooves can be seen {29275417}. Reed–Sternberg–like cells are sometimes observed {15584048}. Small foci of necrosis and mitoses can be seen.

Essential: a tumour comprising spindled to ovoid cells with a storiform, fascicular, or whorled growth pattern; tumour cells with a syncytial appearance; small lymphocytes interspersed with tumour cells; positive immunostaining for two or more FDC markers; negative staining for lymphocyte-specific markers and generally negative staining for S100.
There is no established staging system for FDCS.

FDCS is a low- to intermediate-grade malignancy with a local recurrence rate of 28–40% and a distant metastasis rate of > 25% {9010103; 25917851; 23684177}. Metastasis may occur to other lymph nodes or by haematogenous spread to lung, liver, and bone {23755890}. Surgery is potentially curative for early-stage disease, but recurrence and metastasis can occur many years after initial presentation {10931467}.

A simple stratification based on tumour size and histology was developed to predict the risk of recurrence: low risk, 16% (size < 50 mm, low- or high-grade histology); intermediate risk, 46% (size ≥ 50 mm, low-grade histology), and high risk, 73% (≥ 50 mm, high-grade histology). Mortality is low, except in the high-risk group (45%) {20503450}. Other proposed poor prognostic factors include disseminated disease, extensive necrosis, a high mitotic rate (> 2 mitoses/mm2), and significant nuclear pleomorphism {9010103; 25310210; 22772431; 25917851; 23755890; 20503450}. Patients with complications of paraneoplastic autoimmune multiorgan syndrome experience high morbidity and mortality {30222603}.
